newsitem.title: JORDAN: Palestinian-Israeli violence harms Jordan stocks.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian-Israeli violence harms Jordan stocks.

text.p: Jordanian stocks reeled on Sunday under the influence of Israeli-Palestinian tension despite some buying in select blue chips, brokers said.
The Amman Financial Market 60-share index dropped 0.03 percent to 148.25 points 148.30 points on Saturday, the start of weekly trading.
A total of 334,540 shares changed hands for 618,294 million ($882 million).
"The market slipped slightly on Sunday as it continues to be affected by tension and instability sweeping our region as a result of Israeli-Palestinian unrest," said one dealer.
A total of 55 Palestinians and 14 Israeli soldiers have been killed in protests sparked by Israel's opening Tuesday of a tunnel in Jerusalem near al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third holiest site.
King Hussein will attend an Arab-Israeli summit in Washington early this week, called for by President Clinton to salvage the situation.

"Things are now on hold, but if the crisis is solved, the overall picture for the stock market will look much better as it was starting to pick up in the last weeks and new reforms and legislations are being worked out," added another dealer.
Officials are working on a wider package of reforms aimed at making the market, on a downward trend for two years after a 1992-93 bull run, more efficient, and investor-friendly.

A draft law is due to be put before Jordan's parliament soon which would tighten up regulations on accountability and transparency both for brokers and listed companies on the Amman Financial Market (AFM).

After gradual gains earlier this month that sent the market back above 150 points last week for the first time in four months, shares began to show signs of fatigue in mid-week with stock moving lower in thin volume.
Brokers fear the market may be running out of steam as institutional investors continue to wait in the sidelines and stocks run into profit-taking after the bourse's recent results-driven rally.

The market, one of the most politically sensitive bourses in the region, was hit this year by the breakdown of Middle East peace talks and the delay in implementing a limited oil-for-food deal with Jordan's biggest trading partner Iraq.
Industrials continued to dominate trade on Sunday, followed by banks and services.
Market leader Arab Bank, which propelled the index upwards in the first half of September, remained unchanged at 242 dinars. The Middle East Investment Bank firmed .02 at 1.11 dinars.
Star performer Livestock and Poultry, which has been a focus of investor interest for the fourth week in a row, fell to 0.89 from 0.90.
Jordan Phosphate Mines Company, remained unchanged at 3.20 dinars.
The private Pearl Investable Index of the 45 best performing shares on the exchange fell 0.24 percent to 81.93 points, still 14.21 percent down from the same time last year.
